principles.text: Lower-paying customers churn faster, so price higher and move upmarket instead of cutting prices.
For SaaS, build your network, not your audience. Posting on social media is not marketing.
Run one fast channel and one slow, scalable channel at once, and give each 2-3 months (6+ for SEO) before judging it.
Don't tell me your idea, tell me what problem it solves. Validate with people who have it before building.
Stair-step: start with a simple product on one traffic channel, then make increasingly larger but manageable bets.

sampleQA.question: Should I offer a free plan or a free trial?

answer.text: Default to a free trial. Rob says freemium doesn't work about 90-95% of the time because it removes the motivation to convert.
Freemium is a marketing strategy, not pricing. It needs near-zero support and incremental cost, fast self-serve value, and virality.
In his survey of nearly 700 bootstrapped SaaS, trials requiring a credit card grew at double the rate of no-card trials and had the lowest churn.
Instead of adding a free plan, ask what you'd have to build to justify a 10x price.

sampleQA.question: How should I raise prices on existing customers?

answer.text: Only do it if it lifts MRR by at least 15% (his 'rule of 15'), give 2-6 months notice, and never promise lifetime grandfathering.
Bootstrappers lack the volume to split test pricing, so treat an increase as a reversible experiment on new customers and watch the numbers.
Justify the increase with concrete things you've shipped, and tell customers directly before announcing on social media.

sampleQA.question: My SaaS is stuck at the same MRR. What should I do?

answer.text: Plateaus are math: new MRR divided by monthly revenue churn is your ceiling. $3K new MRR at 5% churn caps you at $60K.
If churn is high, don't chase more leads; you can't outrun it. At 10%+ monthly churn you're effectively pre-PMF.
Segment churn by price tier, channel and cohort, and consider cancelling your lowest plan to move upmarket.
